system.description:
Guerrier

Le Guerrier est un combattant professionnel. Il consacre l’essentiel de son entraînement au maniement des armes, au port de l’armure et aux techniques qui permettent de survivre et de vaincre dans une confrontation directe. Dans les versions précédentes du jeu de rôle des Terres du Milieu et de Rolemaster, il représente déjà le spécialiste martial capable de développer plusieurs catégories d’armes et d’utiliser efficacement les protections lourdes.

La Profession peut représenter un chevalier du Gondor, un cavalier du Rohan, un garde de cité, un mercenaire, un champion de clan, un archer, un combattant khazâd ou un vétéran. La Culture donne sa forme concrète au personnage : un Rohir privilégiera souvent lance, équitation et combat monté ; un Khazad pourra favoriser hache, bouclier et armure ; un Sinda pourra rechercher mobilité, arc et épée.

Caractéristiques primordiales

Les caractéristiques primordiales du Guerrier sont Constitution (Co) et Force (St). La Constitution soutient l’endurance, la résistance aux blessures et aux contraintes prolongées. La Force intervient dans de nombreux entraînements martiaux, le maniement des armes et les efforts physiques liés au combat.

Ces deux caractéristiques doivent recevoir une attention particulière lors de la création du personnage.

Orientation technique

Le Guerrier est un non-utilisateur de sorts. Il ne possède aucune Liste de base. Son développement privilégie les Armes de mêlée, les Armes à distance, le Bouclier, le Combat à mains nues, les Manœuvres en armure, le Combat monté, le Développement corporel, la Protection, le Désarmement, les Attaques multiples, la Course et le Commandement.

Il peut devenir très spécialisé dans une seule arme ou construire une formation martiale plus large. La Profession donne surtout la capacité de consacrer une part importante du développement à plusieurs disciplines de combat sans sacrifier sa robustesse générale.

Combat et équipement

Le Guerrier est naturellement à l’aise avec les armes et l’armure. Un soldat du Gondor peut apprendre la discipline de formation, le bouclier et les protections lourdes ; un cavalier du Rohan associera l’équitation à la lance et à l’épée ; un Khazad des Longues-Barbes pourra privilégier hache, marteau, bouclier et cotte de mailles ; un Corsaire d’Umbar pourra combiner lame, arc et techniques adaptées au combat naval.

Le choix du style de combat relève donc de la Culture, de l’histoire personnelle et de l’équipement disponible plutôt que d’une école unique imposée par la Profession.

Profils de Guerriers

  • Guerrier lourd. Arme de mêlée, Bouclier, Manœuvres en armure et Développement corporel.
  • Archer. Armes à distance, Perception et mobilité.
  • Cavalier. Équitation, Combat monté et arme adaptée au combat à cheval.
  • Champion. Spécialisation poussée dans une arme et techniques de combat avancées.
  • Garde. Protection, Bouclier, Observation et éventuellement Commandement.
  • Capitaine. Compétences martiales, Commandement et aptitudes sociales nécessaires pour diriger une troupe.

Listes de sorts de base

Aucune. Le Guerrier ne possède pas de Liste de base professionnelle. Il peut théoriquement apprendre certaines formes de magie, mais cet apprentissage reste particulièrement coûteux et exceptionnel.

Adaptation RMU / MERP

Nous conservons le châssis mécanique du Fighter RMU : ses coûts de développement, ses groupes d’entraînement au combat et ses compétences professionnelles constituent la base de la Profession.

MERP-RMU rétablit explicitement les caractéristiques primordiales Constitution et Force et replace l’identité du Guerrier dans les traditions militaires de la Terre du Milieu. Sa Race et sa Culture déterminent les armes, les protections et la forme concrète de son entraînement. Son absence de magie reste volontairement nette afin de conserver la distinction traditionnelle entre combattants professionnels et professions magiques.

Fighter

The Fighter is a professional combatant. Most of the profession’s training is devoted to weapons, armour, and the techniques needed to survive and prevail in direct confrontation. In earlier Middle-earth and Rolemaster games, the Fighter already represents the martial specialist able to develop several weapon categories and use heavy protection effectively.

The Profession may represent a knight of Gondor, a rider of Rohan, a city guard, mercenary, clan champion, archer, Khazâd warrior, or veteran. Culture gives the character a concrete form: a Rohir will often favour spear, riding, and mounted combat; a Khazad may favour axe, shield, and armour; a Sinda may seek mobility, bow, and sword.

Prime Stats

The Fighter’s Prime Stats are Constitution (Co) and Strength (St). Constitution supports endurance, resistance to wounds, and prolonged physical hardship. Strength naturally contributes to many martial disciplines, weapon use, and strenuous physical effort.

These two Stats deserve particular attention during character creation.

Technical orientation

The Fighter is a non-spell-user and has no Base Lists. Development favours Melee Weapons, Ranged Weapons, Shield, Unarmed Combat, Maneuvering in Armor, Mounted Combat, Body Development, Protect, Disarm, Multiple Attacks, Running, and Leadership.

A Fighter may become highly specialized in one weapon or build a broader martial training. The Profession’s main strength is the ability to invest heavily in several combat disciplines without giving up overall physical resilience.

Combat and equipment

Fighters are naturally comfortable with weapons and armour. A Gondorian soldier may learn formation discipline, shield, and heavy armour; a rider of Rohan may combine riding with spear and sword; a Longbeard Khazad may favour axe, hammer, shield, and mail; a Corsair of Umbar may combine blade, bow, and techniques suited to fighting at sea.

The choice of fighting style therefore comes from Culture, personal history, and available equipment rather than from a single school imposed by the Profession.

Fighter profiles

  • Heavy Fighter. Melee weapon, Shield, Maneuvering in Armor, and Body Development.
  • Archer. Ranged Weapons, Perception, and mobility.
  • Rider. Riding, Mounted Combat, and a weapon suited to fighting from horseback.
  • Champion. Deep specialization in one main weapon and advanced combat techniques.
  • Guard. Protect, Shield, Observation, and possibly Leadership.
  • Captain. Martial skills combined with Leadership and the social abilities needed to command troops.

Base Spell Lists

None. The Fighter has no professional Base Spell List. A Fighter can theoretically learn some forms of magic, but doing so is unusually costly and represents an exceptional path.

RMU / MERP adaptation

We retain the RMU Fighter mechanical chassis: its development costs, combat training groups, and professional skills remain the foundation of the Profession.

MERP-RMU explicitly restores Constitution and Strength as the Prime Stats and places the Fighter within the military traditions of Middle-earth. Race and Culture determine weapons, protection, and the concrete form of training. The deliberate absence of magic preserves the traditional distinction between professional warriors and magical professions.

talents.name: Darkvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient jusqu’à 10 pieds sans pénalité, même dans l’obscurité totale non magique.

talents.name: Nightvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient dans une faible lumière aussi bien qu’un Humain en plein jour. Toutes les pénalités dues à l’obscurité sont réduites de 40, sauf dans l’obscurité absolue.

talents.name: Inept
talents.description: En raison de leur densité et de leur faible affinité avec l’eau libre, les Khazâd subissent une pénalité de −25 aux Jets d’Endurance effectués en nageant.

talents.name: Fast Healer
talents.description: Les Khazâd récupèrent rapidement. Les temps de récupération naturelle sont divisés par deux.

talents.name: Tough
talents.description: Les Khazâd sont exceptionnellement robustes et résistants à la douleur. Leurs points de vie de base sont augmentés de 5.

system.description:
Khazâd — Naugrim

Les Khazâd, appelés Naugrim par les Elfes, descendent des Sept Pères façonnés dans la pierre par le Vala Aulë. Les Nains nomment Aulë Mahal, « le Créateur ». Il est le maître des métiers, de la pierre, des métaux et des forges. Les sept lignées issues des Pères s’établirent dans des régions différentes, mais toujours dans ou près des montagnes, que les Khazâd considèrent comme sacrées.

Aulë façonna les Nains avant l’éveil des Elfes, mais Eru lui imposa de différer leur éveil jusqu’après l’apparition des Premiers-Nés. Les Sept Pères s’éveillèrent ensuite en des lieux distincts. Le plus célèbre fut Durin l’Immortel, qui s’éveilla sous le mont Gundabad avant de gagner le sud et de fonder Khazad-dûm.

Les Sept Maisons

Les descendants des Sept Pères formèrent les grandes Maisons naines. Au fil des Âges, leurs membres se dispersèrent dans toute la Terre du Milieu, fondant ou occupant des cités souterraines, des mines et des établissements de montagne.

Chaque Maison possède ses propres lignées, traditions, dialectes, préférences artisanales et histoires. La Race Khazâd représente ce qui est commun à tous les Nains ; les différences entre la Maison de Durin, les Barbes-de-Feu, les Torses-Larges et les autres lignées doivent être portées par les Cultures.

Apparence

Les Khazâd sont petits, trapus et puissamment bâtis. Leur ossature est massive, leurs épaules larges et leurs membres particulièrement forts. Leur poids est élevé par rapport à leur taille. Les hommes portent presque toujours une barbe, souvent longue et entretenue selon les usages de leur Maison.

Les femmes naines sont moins nombreuses que les hommes et quittent rarement les demeures de leur peuple. Elles peuvent également porter une barbe, ce qui contribue à la difficulté qu’éprouvent les étrangers à distinguer immédiatement les sexes. La couleur des cheveux, de la peau et des yeux varie selon les lignées.

Longévité et maturité

Les Khazâd vivent plusieurs siècles. Ils atteignent leur maturité plus lentement que les Hommes et conservent longtemps leur force et leur vigueur. Leur longévité leur permet de consacrer des décennies à un ouvrage, de connaître plusieurs générations humaines et de conserver très longtemps la mémoire d’une dette, d’un serment ou d’une offense.

Ils restent cependant mortels. Leurs traditions enseignent qu’après la mort ils sont rassemblés auprès de Mahal et qu’ils auront un rôle à jouer dans la restauration d’Arda après sa fin.

Endurance et résistance

Les Nains sont réputés pour leur endurance. Ils supportent bien les longues marches, le travail prolongé, les charges lourdes, le froid, la chaleur et les privations. Leur constitution les rend également plus résistants que les Hommes ordinaires aux maladies et aux poisons.

Cette robustesse constitue l’un de leurs principaux traits raciaux. Elle ne doit toutefois pas être confondue avec une immunité : les blessures graves, les maladies puissantes et les poisons élaborés peuvent toujours les tuer.

Vision et sens de la pierre

Les Khazâd sont adaptés à la vie souterraine et voient bien dans une faible lumière. Ils savent se déplacer et travailler dans des galeries où des Hommes auraient besoin d’un éclairage important.

Ils possèdent également un sens remarquable de la pierre et des ouvrages souterrains. Un Nain expérimenté reconnaît les différences entre roche naturelle et maçonnerie, évalue la stabilité d’une galerie et remarque facilement des caractéristiques inhabituelles dans un mur, un tunnel ou un ouvrage de pierre. Cette aptitude doit être représentée comme un trait racial commun, sans remplacer les véritables compétences de mineur, architecte ou tailleur de pierre.

Tempérament et mémoire

Les Khazâd ont une réputation de robustesse, de pragmatisme, d’obstination et de loyauté. Ils sont généralement prudents avec les étrangers et accordent une grande valeur aux engagements clairement formulés.

Ils se souviennent longtemps des services rendus comme des offenses. Un accord, une dette, un vol ou un serment peuvent rester importants pendant plusieurs générations. Cette mémoire nourrit leur réputation de rancune, mais elle explique aussi la solidité de leurs amitiés et de leurs alliances lorsqu’elles ont été réellement établies.

Lignée, famille et autorité

La famille, le clan et la Maison occupent une place centrale dans la société naine. Un Khazâd connaît généralement sa généalogie et les principaux événements qui concernent ses ancêtres. Les métiers et certains secrets artisanaux sont souvent transmis au sein des familles.

Les rois des grandes Maisons représentent la continuité de leur lignée et de leurs demeures. Chez les Longues-Barbes, la figure de Durin occupe une place particulière. Le mariage est monogame et durable ; les enfants sont relativement rares et fortement protégés.

Artisanat et mines

Les Khazâd sont parmi les meilleurs artisans de la Terre du Milieu. Ils excellent dans la forge, la métallurgie, l’armurerie, la taille de pierre, l’architecture, la joaillerie, l’ingénierie et l’exploitation minière. Ils recherchent les gemmes et les métaux précieux et les transforment en outils, armes, armures, bijoux et objets d’une grande qualité.

Leur artisanat privilégie la solidité et la durée. Un ouvrage nain est généralement conçu pour traverser plusieurs générations. Le travail de la matière est aussi étroitement lié à leur respect pour Mahal.

Demeures

Les Khazâd privilégient les hautes terres rocheuses, les cavernes et les cités taillées dans la montagne. Khazad-dûm fut la plus célèbre de leurs demeures, mais Nogrod, Belegost, Erebor, les Montagnes Grises, les Collines de Fer et de nombreux établissements moins connus appartiennent également à leur histoire.

Leurs grandes demeures associent mines, ateliers, halls, réserves, fortifications, routes souterraines et espaces de vie. Elles sont souvent conçues pour pouvoir être défendues dans des passages étroits.

Langue et écriture

Le khuzdul fut enseigné aux Nains par Mahal. Ils le gardent jalousement et le révèlent rarement aux étrangers. Les véritables noms khuzdul sont généralement secrets, et les Nains utilisent souvent des noms provenant des langues de leurs voisins lorsqu’ils traitent avec les autres peuples.

Ils utilisent volontiers les cirth pour graver des inscriptions sur la pierre, le métal, les armes, les portes et les tombes. L’écriture gravée convient à leur attachement à la permanence et à la mémoire.

Religion

Les Khazâd reconnaissent Eru comme le Créateur suprême et honorent profondément Mahal. Leur religion n’est généralement pas organisée autour d’un clergé visible. Elle s’exprime surtout par le respect des ancêtres, des tombeaux, des grandes demeures, des métiers et des œuvres durables.

Les forges, les halls ancestraux et les sépultures royales peuvent avoir une forte dimension sacrée. La création d’un objet exceptionnel peut elle-même être considérée comme une manière d’honorer Mahal.

Armes, armures et guerre

Les Nains utilisent de nombreuses armes, mais les haches, marteaux, masses, épées, arbalètes et armes d’hast sont particulièrement courantes. Ils excellent dans la fabrication et le port de la maille et des armures lourdes. Leur force et leur endurance leur permettent de conserver une bonne efficacité sous des protections qui ralentiraient fortement d’autres peuples.

Ils sont particulièrement dangereux dans les combats défensifs, les tunnels, les portes, les ponts et les défilés. Ils savent exploiter les passages étroits, les formations serrées, les boucliers, les éboulements et les ouvrages souterrains.

Relations et ennemis

Les relations avec les Elfes ont alterné entre coopération, commerce et conflits anciens. Les Noldor et les Khazâd ont parfois entretenu des relations particulièrement fécondes en raison de leur intérêt commun pour l’artisanat et les matériaux. Les tensions avec certains Sindar furent plus durables, notamment après les événements liés au Nauglamír.

Les Nains commercent volontiers avec les Hommes lorsqu’ils les jugent fiables et entretiennent généralement des rapports pacifiques avec les Hobbits. Leurs ennemis traditionnels comprennent surtout les Orcs, les Trolls, les Dragons et les créatures des profondeurs. Leur haine des Orcs est ancienne et liée aux guerres pour les montagnes, les mines et les forteresses.

Résistance à l’Ombre

Les Khazâd sont difficiles à soumettre par la domination mentale. Les Anneaux de Pouvoir donnés aux Nains ne firent pas d’eux des esclaves de Sauron comme les Neuf le firent des Hommes. Ils accrurent plutôt leur désir de richesse et leur avidité.

Cette résistance n’empêche pas la corruption par la cupidité, l’orgueil, la rancune ou l’obsession. La Race ne doit donc pas être considérée comme moralement protégée de l’Ombre.

Professions et place dans la création de personnage

La Race Khazâd — Naugrim est disponible durant les quatre Âges. Elle doit représenter les caractéristiques communes : petite taille, forte constitution, endurance, résistances, vision en faible lumière et sens de la pierre.

Les compétences de forge, de mine, de commerce, de guerre ou de magie doivent être précisées par la Culture. Après le choix de la Race, le joueur sélectionne une Maison ou une Culture correspondant à son origine, comme la Maison de Durin — Longues-Barbes ou les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár — Barbes-de-Feu et Torses-Larges.

Ils excellent dans la fabrication et le port de la maille et des armures lourdes. Les Noldor et les Khazâd ont parfois entretenu des relations particulièrement fécondes en raison de leur intérêt commun pour l’artisanat et les matériaux. Professions et place dans la création de personnage

Après le choix de la Race, le joueur sélectionne une Maison ou une Culture correspondant à son origine, comme la Maison de Durin — Longues-Barbes ou les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár — Barbes-de-Feu et Torses-Larges.

Khazâd — Naugrim

The Khazâd, called Naugrim by the Elves, descend from the Seven Fathers fashioned from stone by the Vala Aulë. The Dwarves call Aulë Mahal, “the Maker”. He is the master of crafts, stone, metals and forges. The seven lineages descended from the Fathers settled in different regions, but always in or near mountains, which the Khazâd regard as sacred.

Aulë fashioned the Dwarves before the awakening of the Elves, but Eru required him to delay their awakening until after the appearance of the Firstborn. The Seven Fathers later awoke in different places. The most famous was Durin the Deathless, who awoke beneath Mount Gundabad before travelling south and founding Khazad-dûm.

The Seven Houses

Appearance

The Khazâd are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their bones are massive, their shoulders broad and their limbs exceptionally strong. They are heavy for their height. Men almost always wear beards, often long and maintained according to the customs of their House.

Dwarven women are fewer than men and rarely leave the dwellings of their people. They may also wear beards, which contributes to the difficulty outsiders have in immediately distinguishing the sexes. Hair, skin and eye colour vary according to lineage.

Longevity and maturity

The Khazâd live for several centuries. They reach maturity more slowly than Men and retain their strength and vigour for a long time. Their longevity allows them to devote decades to a work, know several human generations and preserve the memory of a debt, oath or insult for a very long time.

They nevertheless remain mortal. Their traditions teach that after death they are gathered to Mahal and that they will have a part to play in the restoration of Arda after its end.

Endurance and resistance

Dwarves are renowned for their endurance. They tolerate long marches, prolonged labour, heavy loads, cold, heat and deprivation well. Their constitution also makes them more resistant than ordinary Men to diseases and poisons.

This robustness is one of their principal racial traits. It should not, however, be confused with immunity: severe wounds, powerful diseases and sophisticated poisons can still kill them.

Vision and sense of stone

The Khazâd are adapted to underground life and see well in dim light. They know how to move and work in galleries where Men would require substantial illumination.

They also possess a remarkable sense for stone and underground works. An experienced Dwarf recognises the difference between natural rock and masonry, judges the stability of a gallery and readily notices unusual features in a wall, tunnel or stone construction. This ability should be represented as a common racial trait without replacing true skills in mining, architecture or stonecutting.

Temperament and memory

The Khazâd have a reputation for toughness, pragmatism, stubbornness and loyalty. They are generally cautious with strangers and place great value on clearly stated commitments.

They remember services rendered as well as offences for a long time. An agreement, debt, theft or oath may remain important for several generations. This memory feeds their reputation for bearing grudges, but also explains the solidity of their friendships and alliances once these have truly been established.

Lineage, family and authority

Family, clan and House occupy a central place in Dwarven society. A Khazâd generally knows their genealogy and the principal events concerning their ancestors. Crafts and certain secrets of workmanship are often passed down within families.

The kings of the great Houses represent the continuity of their lineages and dwellings. Among the Longbeards, the figure of Durin holds a special place. Marriage is monogamous and enduring; children are relatively rare and fiercely protected.

Craft and mining

The Khazâd are among the finest craftsmen of Middle-earth. They excel in smithcraft, metallurgy, armour-making, stonecutting, architecture, jewellery, engineering and mining. They seek gems and precious metals and transform them into tools, weapons, armour, jewellery and objects of exceptional quality.

Their craftsmanship favours strength and durability. A Dwarven work is generally intended to last for several generations. The working of matter is also closely connected to their reverence for Mahal.

Dwellings

The Khazâd favour rocky highlands, caverns and cities carved into mountains. Khazad-dûm was the most famous of their dwellings, but Nogrod, Belegost, Erebor, the Grey Mountains, the Iron Hills and many lesser-known settlements also belong to their history.

Their great mansions combine mines, workshops, halls, stores, fortifications, underground roads and living spaces. They are often designed so that they can be defended through narrow passages.

Language and writing

Khuzdul was taught to the Dwarves by Mahal. They guard it jealously and rarely reveal it to outsiders. True Khuzdul names are generally secret, and Dwarves often use names drawn from the languages of their neighbours when dealing with other peoples.

They readily use the Cirth to carve inscriptions into stone, metal, weapons, doors and tombs. Engraved writing suits their attachment to permanence and memory.

Religion

The Khazâd acknowledge Eru as the supreme Creator and deeply honour Mahal. Their religion is generally not organised around a visible clergy. It is expressed chiefly through reverence for ancestors, tombs, great dwellings, crafts and enduring works.

Forges, ancestral halls and royal tombs can possess a strong sacred dimension. The creation of an exceptional object may itself be regarded as a way of honouring Mahal.

Weapons, armour and war

Dwarves use many weapons, but axes, hammers, maces, swords, crossbows and polearms are especially common. They excel in making and wearing mail and heavy armour. Their strength and endurance allow them to remain effective under protection that would greatly slow other peoples.

They are particularly dangerous in defensive fighting, tunnels, gates, bridges and narrow passes. They know how to exploit confined approaches, close formations, shields, rockfalls and underground works.

Relations and enemies

Relations with the Elves have alternated between cooperation, trade and ancient conflict. The Noldor and the Khazâd have sometimes maintained especially fruitful relations because of their shared interest in craft and materials. Tensions with certain Sindar lasted longer, especially after the events surrounding the Nauglamír.

Dwarves willingly trade with Men they consider reliable and generally maintain peaceful relations with Hobbits. Their traditional enemies include chiefly Orcs, Trolls, Dragons and creatures of the deep. Their hatred of Orcs is ancient and rooted in wars over mountains, mines and fortresses.

Resistance to the Shadow

The Khazâd are difficult to subdue through mental domination. The Rings of Power given to the Dwarves did not make them slaves of Sauron as the Nine did the Men who bore them. Instead, they increased their desire for wealth and their greed.

This resistance does not prevent corruption through avarice, pride, resentment or obsession. The Race should therefore not be regarded as morally protected from the Shadow.

Professions and place in character creation

The Khazâd — Naugrim Race is available throughout all four Ages. It should represent the shared traits of the Dwarves: short stature, strong constitution, endurance, resistances, vision in dim light and sense of stone.

talents.name: Darkvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient jusqu’à 10 pieds sans pénalité, même dans l’obscurité totale non magique.

talents.name: Nightvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient dans une faible lumière aussi bien qu’un Humain en plein jour. Toutes les pénalités dues à l’obscurité sont réduites de 40, sauf dans l’obscurité absolue.

talents.name: Inept
talents.description: En raison de leur densité et de leur faible affinité avec l’eau libre, les Khazâd subissent une pénalité de −25 aux Jets d’Endurance effectués en nageant.

talents.name: Fast Healer
talents.description: Les Khazâd récupèrent rapidement. Les temps de récupération naturelle sont divisés par deux.

talents.name: Tough
talents.description: Les Khazâd sont exceptionnellement robustes et résistants à la douleur. Leurs points de vie de base sont augmentés de 5.

Les Noldor et les Khazâd ont parfois entretenu des relations particulièrement fécondes en raison de leur intérêt commun pour l’artisanat et les matériaux. Khazâd — Naugrim

The Khazâd, called Naugrim by the Elves, descend from the Seven Fathers fashioned from stone by the Vala Aulë. The Dwarves call Aulë Mahal, “the Maker”. He is the master of crafts, stone, metals and forges. The seven lineages descended from the Fathers settled in different regions, but always in or near mountains, which the Khazâd regard as sacred.

Aulë fashioned the Dwarves before the awakening of the Elves, but Eru required him to delay their awakening until after the appearance of the Firstborn. The Seven Fathers later awoke in different places. The most famous was Durin the Deathless, who awoke beneath Mount Gundabad before travelling south and founding Khazad-dûm.

The Seven Houses

Appearance

The Khazâd are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their bones are massive, their shoulders broad and their limbs exceptionally strong. They are heavy for their height. Men almost always wear beards, often long and maintained according to the customs of their House.

Dwarven women are fewer than men and rarely leave the dwellings of their people. They may also wear beards, which contributes to the difficulty outsiders have in immediately distinguishing the sexes. Hair, skin and eye colour vary according to lineage.

Longevity and maturity

The Khazâd live for several centuries. They reach maturity more slowly than Men and retain their strength and vigour for a long time. Their longevity allows them to devote decades to a work, know several human generations and preserve the memory of a debt, oath or insult for a very long time.

They nevertheless remain mortal. Their traditions teach that after death they are gathered to Mahal and that they will have a part to play in the restoration of Arda after its end.

Endurance and resistance

Dwarves are renowned for their endurance. They tolerate long marches, prolonged labour, heavy loads, cold, heat and deprivation well. Their constitution also makes them more resistant than ordinary Men to diseases and poisons.

This robustness is one of their principal racial traits. It should not, however, be confused with immunity: severe wounds, powerful diseases and sophisticated poisons can still kill them.

Vision and sense of stone

The Khazâd are adapted to underground life and see well in dim light. They know how to move and work in galleries where Men would require substantial illumination.

They also possess a remarkable sense for stone and underground works. An experienced Dwarf recognises the difference between natural rock and masonry, judges the stability of a gallery and readily notices unusual features in a wall, tunnel or stone construction. This ability should be represented as a common racial trait without replacing true skills in mining, architecture or stonecutting.

Temperament and memory

The Khazâd have a reputation for toughness, pragmatism, stubbornness and loyalty. They are generally cautious with strangers and place great value on clearly stated commitments.

They remember services rendered as well as offences for a long time. An agreement, debt, theft or oath may remain important for several generations. This memory feeds their reputation for bearing grudges, but also explains the solidity of their friendships and alliances once these have truly been established.

Lineage, family and authority

Family, clan and House occupy a central place in Dwarven society. A Khazâd generally knows their genealogy and the principal events concerning their ancestors. Crafts and certain secrets of workmanship are often passed down within families.

The kings of the great Houses represent the continuity of their lineages and dwellings. Among the Longbeards, the figure of Durin holds a special place. Marriage is monogamous and enduring; children are relatively rare and fiercely protected.

Craft and mining

They seek gems and precious metals and transform them into tools, weapons, armour, jewellery and objects of exceptional quality.

Their craftsmanship favours strength and durability. A Dwarven work is generally intended to last for several generations. The working of matter is also closely connected to their reverence for Mahal.

The Khazâd favour rocky highlands, caverns and cities carved into mountains. Khazad-dûm was the most famous of their dwellings, but Nogrod, Belegost, Erebor, the Grey Mountains, the Iron Hills and many lesser-known settlements also belong to their history.

Their great mansions combine mines, workshops, halls, stores, fortifications, underground roads and living spaces. They are often designed so that they can be defended through narrow passages.

Khuzdul was taught to the Dwarves by Mahal. They guard it jealously and rarely reveal it to outsiders. True Khuzdul names are generally secret, and Dwarves often use names drawn from the languages of their neighbours when dealing with other peoples.

They readily use the Cirth to carve inscriptions into stone, metal, weapons, doors and tombs. Engraved writing suits their attachment to permanence and memory.

The Khazâd acknowledge Eru as the supreme Creator and deeply honour Mahal. Their religion is generally not organised around a visible clergy. It is expressed chiefly through reverence for ancestors, tombs, great dwellings, crafts and enduring works.

Forges, ancestral halls and royal tombs can possess a strong sacred dimension. The creation of an exceptional object may itself be regarded as a way of honouring Mahal.

Weapons, armour and war

Dwarves use many weapons, but axes, hammers, maces, swords, crossbows and polearms are especially common. They excel in making and wearing mail and heavy armour. Their strength and endurance allow them to remain effective under protection that would greatly slow other peoples.

They are particularly dangerous in defensive fighting, tunnels, gates, bridges and narrow passes. They know how to exploit confined approaches, close formations, shields, rockfalls and underground works.

Relations with the Elves have alternated between cooperation, trade and ancient conflict. The Noldor and the Khazâd have sometimes maintained especially fruitful relations because of their shared interest in craft and materials. Tensions with certain Sindar lasted longer, especially after the events surrounding the Nauglamír.

Dwarves willingly trade with Men they consider reliable and generally maintain peaceful relations with Hobbits. Their traditional enemies include chiefly Orcs, Trolls, Dragons and creatures of the deep. Their hatred of Orcs is ancient and rooted in wars over mountains, mines and fortresses.

Resistance to the Shadow

The Khazâd are difficult to subdue through mental domination. The Rings of Power given to the Dwarves did not make them slaves of Sauron as the Nine did the Men who bore them. Instead, they increased their desire for wealth and their greed.

This resistance does not prevent corruption through avarice, pride, resentment or obsession. The Race should therefore not be regarded as morally protected from the Shadow.

Professions and place in character creation

The Khazâd — Naugrim Race is available throughout all four Ages. It should represent the shared traits of the Dwarves: short stature, strong constitution, endurance, resistances, vision in dim light and sense of stone.

talents.name: Darkvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient jusqu’à 10 pieds sans pénalité, même dans l’obscurité totale non magique.

talents.name: Nightvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient dans une faible lumière aussi bien qu’un Humain en plein jour. Toutes les pénalités dues à l’obscurité sont réduites de 40, sauf dans l’obscurité absolue.

talents.name: Inept
talents.description: En raison de leur densité et de leur faible affinité avec l’eau libre, les Khazâd subissent une pénalité de −25 aux Jets d’Endurance effectués en nageant.

talents.name: Fast Healer
talents.description: Les Khazâd récupèrent rapidement. Les temps de récupération naturelle sont divisés par deux.

talents.name: Tough
talents.description: Les Khazâd sont exceptionnellement robustes et résistants à la douleur. Leurs points de vie de base sont augmentés de 5.

Ils utilisent volontiers les cirth pour graver des inscriptions sur la pierre, le métal, les armes, les portes et les tombes. L’écriture gravée convient à leur attachement à la permanence et à la mémoire.

Religion

Les Khazâd reconnaissent Eru comme le Créateur suprême et honorent profondément Mahal. Leur religion n’est généralement pas organisée autour d’un clergé visible. Elle s’exprime surtout par le respect des ancêtres, des tombeaux, des grandes demeures, des métiers et des œuvres durables.

Les forges, les halls ancestraux et les sépultures royales peuvent avoir une forte dimension sacrée. La création d’un objet exceptionnel peut elle-même être considérée comme une manière d’honorer Mahal.

Armes, armures et guerre

Les Nains utilisent de nombreuses armes, mais les haches, marteaux, masses, épées, arbalètes et armes d’hast sont particulièrement courantes. Ils excellent dans la fabrication et le port de la maille et des armures lourdes. Leur force et leur endurance leur permettent de conserver une bonne efficacité sous des protections qui ralentiraient fortement d’autres peuples.

Ils sont particulièrement dangereux dans les combats défensifs, les tunnels, les portes, les ponts et les défilés. Ils savent exploiter les passages étroits, les formations serrées, les boucliers, les éboulements et les ouvrages souterrains.

Relations et ennemis

Les relations avec les Elfes ont alterné entre coopération, commerce et conflits anciens. Les Noldor et les Khazâd ont parfois entretenu des relations particulièrement fécondes en raison de leur intérêt commun pour l’artisanat et les matériaux. Les tensions avec certains Sindar furent plus durables, notamment après les événements liés au Nauglamír.

Les Nains commercent volontiers avec les Hommes lorsqu’ils les jugent fiables et entretiennent généralement des rapports pacifiques avec les Hobbits. Leurs ennemis traditionnels comprennent surtout les Orcs, les Trolls, les Dragons et les créatures des profondeurs. Leur haine des Orcs est ancienne et liée aux guerres pour les montagnes, les mines et les forteresses.

Résistance à l’Ombre

Les Khazâd sont difficiles à soumettre par la domination mentale. Les Anneaux de Pouvoir donnés aux Nains ne firent pas d’eux des esclaves de Sauron comme les Neuf le firent des Hommes. Ils accrurent plutôt leur désir de richesse et leur avidité.

Cette résistance n’empêche pas la corruption par la cupidité, l’orgueil, la rancune ou l’obsession. La Race ne doit donc pas être considérée comme moralement protégée de l’Ombre.

Professions et place dans la création de personnage

La Race Khazâd — Naugrim est disponible durant les quatre Âges. Elle doit représenter les caractéristiques communes : petite taille, forte constitution, endurance, résistances, vision en faible lumière et sens de la pierre.

Les compétences de forge, de mine, de commerce, de guerre ou de magie doivent être précisées par la Culture. Après le choix de la Race, le joueur sélectionne une Maison ou une Culture correspondant à son origine, comme la Maison de Durin — Longues-Barbes ou les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár — Barbes-de-Feu et Torses-Larges.

Khazâd — Naugrim

The Khazâd, called Naugrim by the Elves, descend from the Seven Fathers fashioned from stone by the Vala Aulë. The Dwarves call Aulë Mahal, “the Maker”. He is the master of crafts, stone, metals and forges. The seven lineages descended from the Fathers settled in different regions, but always in or near mountains, which the Khazâd regard as sacred.

Aulë fashioned the Dwarves before the awakening of the Elves, but Eru required him to delay their awakening until after the appearance of the Firstborn. The Seven Fathers later awoke in different places. The most famous was Durin the Deathless, who awoke beneath Mount Gundabad before travelling south and founding Khazad-dûm.

The Seven Houses

The descendants of the Seven Fathers formed the great Dwarven Houses. Over the Ages, their members spread throughout Middle-earth, founding or occupying underground cities, mines and mountain settlements.

Each House possesses its own lineages, traditions, dialects, preferred crafts and histories. The Khazâd Race represents what is shared by all Dwarves; differences between the House of Durin, the Firebeards, the Broadbeams and the other lineages should be carried by Cultures.

Appearance

The Khazâd are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their bones are massive, their shoulders broad and their limbs exceptionally strong. They are heavy for their height. Men almost always wear beards, often long and maintained according to the customs of their House.

Dwarven women are fewer than men and rarely leave the dwellings of their people. They may also wear beards, which contributes to the difficulty outsiders have in immediately distinguishing the sexes. Hair, skin and eye colour vary according to lineage.

Longevity and maturity

The Khazâd live for several centuries. They reach maturity more slowly than Men and retain their strength and vigour for a long time. Their longevity allows them to devote decades to a work, know several human generations and preserve the memory of a debt, oath or insult for a very long time.

They nevertheless remain mortal. Their traditions teach that after death they are gathered to Mahal and that they will have a part to play in the restoration of Arda after its end.

Endurance and resistance

Dwarves are renowned for their endurance. They tolerate long marches, prolonged labour, heavy loads, cold, heat and deprivation well. Their constitution also makes them more resistant than ordinary Men to diseases and poisons.

This robustness is one of their principal racial traits. It should not, however, be confused with immunity: severe wounds, powerful diseases and sophisticated poisons can still kill them.

Vision and sense of stone

The Khazâd are adapted to underground life and see well in dim light. They know how to move and work in galleries where Men would require substantial illumination.

They also possess a remarkable sense for stone and underground works. An experienced Dwarf recognises the difference between natural rock and masonry, judges the stability of a gallery and readily notices unusual features in a wall, tunnel or stone construction. This ability should be represented as a common racial trait without replacing true skills in mining, architecture or stonecutting.

Temperament and memory

The Khazâd have a reputation for toughness, pragmatism, stubbornness and loyalty. They are generally cautious with strangers and place great value on clearly stated commitments.

They remember services rendered as well as offences for a long time. An agreement, debt, theft or oath may remain important for several generations. This memory feeds their reputation for bearing grudges, but also explains the solidity of their friendships and alliances once these have truly been established.

Lineage, family and authority

Family, clan and House occupy a central place in Dwarven society. A Khazâd generally knows their genealogy and the principal events concerning their ancestors. Crafts and certain secrets of workmanship are often passed down within families.

The kings of the great Houses represent the continuity of their lineages and dwellings. Among the Longbeards, the figure of Durin holds a special place. Marriage is monogamous and enduring; children are relatively rare and fiercely protected.

Craft and mining

The Khazâd are among the finest craftsmen of Middle-earth. They excel in smithcraft, metallurgy, armour-making, stonecutting, architecture, jewellery, engineering and mining. They seek gems and precious metals and transform them into tools, weapons, armour, jewellery and objects of exceptional quality.

Their craftsmanship favours strength and durability. A Dwarven work is generally intended to last for several generations. The working of matter is also closely connected to their reverence for Mahal.

Dwellings

The Khazâd favour rocky highlands, caverns and cities carved into mountains. Khazad-dûm was the most famous of their dwellings, but Nogrod, Belegost, Erebor, the Grey Mountains, the Iron Hills and many lesser-known settlements also belong to their history.

Their great mansions combine mines, workshops, halls, stores, fortifications, underground roads and living spaces. They are often designed so that they can be defended through narrow passages.

Language and writing

Khuzdul was taught to the Dwarves by Mahal. They guard it jealously and rarely reveal it to outsiders. True Khuzdul names are generally secret, and Dwarves often use names drawn from the languages of their neighbours when dealing with other peoples.

They readily use the Cirth to carve inscriptions into stone, metal, weapons, doors and tombs. Engraved writing suits their attachment to permanence and memory.

Religion

The Khazâd acknowledge Eru as the supreme Creator and deeply honour Mahal. Their religion is generally not organised around a visible clergy. It is expressed chiefly through reverence for ancestors, tombs, great dwellings, crafts and enduring works.

Forges, ancestral halls and royal tombs can possess a strong sacred dimension. The creation of an exceptional object may itself be regarded as a way of honouring Mahal.

Weapons, armour and war

Dwarves use many weapons, but axes, hammers, maces, swords, crossbows and polearms are especially common. They excel in making and wearing mail and heavy armour. Their strength and endurance allow them to remain effective under protection that would greatly slow other peoples.

They are particularly dangerous in defensive fighting, tunnels, gates, bridges and narrow passes. They know how to exploit confined approaches, close formations, shields, rockfalls and underground works.

Relations and enemies

Relations with the Elves have alternated between cooperation, trade and ancient conflict. The Noldor and the Khazâd have sometimes maintained especially fruitful relations because of their shared interest in craft and materials. Tensions with certain Sindar lasted longer, especially after the events surrounding the Nauglamír.

Dwarves willingly trade with Men they consider reliable and generally maintain peaceful relations with Hobbits. Their traditional enemies include chiefly Orcs, Trolls, Dragons and creatures of the deep. Their hatred of Orcs is ancient and rooted in wars over mountains, mines and fortresses.

Resistance to the Shadow

The Khazâd are difficult to subdue through mental domination. The Rings of Power given to the Dwarves did not make them slaves of Sauron as the Nine did the Men who bore them. Instead, they increased their desire for wealth and their greed.

This resistance does not prevent corruption through avarice, pride, resentment or obsession. The Race should therefore not be regarded as morally protected from the Shadow.

Professions and place in character creation

The Khazâd — Naugrim Race is available throughout all four Ages. It should represent the shared traits of the Dwarves: short stature, strong constitution, endurance, resistances, vision in dim light and sense of stone.

Skills in smithing, mining, trade, warfare or magic should be specified by Culture. After choosing the Race, the player selects a House or Culture corresponding to the character’s origin, such as the House of Durin — Longbeards or the Houses of Dwálin and Thrár — Firebeards and Broadbeams.

talents.name: Darkvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient jusqu’à 10 pieds sans pénalité, même dans l’obscurité totale non magique.

talents.name: Nightvision
talents.description: Les Khazâd voient dans une faible lumière aussi bien qu’un Humain en plein jour. Toutes les pénalités dues à l’obscurité sont réduites de 40, sauf dans l’obscurité absolue.

talents.name: Inept
talents.description: En raison de leur densité et de leur faible affinité avec l’eau libre, les Khazâd subissent une pénalité de −25 aux Jets d’Endurance effectués en nageant.

talents.name: Fast Healer
talents.description: Les Khazâd récupèrent rapidement. Les temps de récupération naturelle sont divisés par deux.

talents.name: Tough
talents.description: Les Khazâd sont exceptionnellement robustes et résistants à la douleur. Leurs points de vie de base sont augmentés de 5.

Apparence

Elles peuvent également porter une barbe, ce qui contribue à la difficulté qu’éprouvent les étrangers à distinguer immédiatement les sexes. Les Khazâd reconnaissent Eru comme le Créateur suprême et honorent profondément Mahal. Leur religion n’est généralement pas organisée autour d’un clergé visible. Elle s’exprime surtout par le respect des ancêtres, des tombeaux, des grandes demeures, des métiers et des œuvres durables.

Les forges, les halls ancestraux et les sépultures royales peuvent avoir une forte dimension sacrée. La création d’un objet exceptionnel peut elle-même être considérée comme une manière d’honorer Mahal.

Armes, armures et guerre

Les Nains utilisent de nombreuses armes, mais les haches, marteaux, masses, épées, arbalètes et armes d’hast sont particulièrement courantes. Ils excellent dans la fabrication et le port de la maille et des armures lourdes. Leur force et leur endurance leur permettent de conserver une bonne efficacité sous des protections qui ralentiraient fortement d’autres peuples.

Ils sont particulièrement dangereux dans les combats défensifs, les tunnels, les portes, les ponts et les défilés. Ils savent exploiter les passages étroits, les formations serrées, les boucliers, les éboulements et les ouvrages souterrains.

Relations et ennemis

Les relations avec les Elfes ont alterné entre coopération, commerce et conflits anciens. Les Noldor et les Khazâd ont parfois entretenu des relations particulièrement fécondes en raison de leur intérêt commun pour l’artisanat et les matériaux. Les tensions avec certains Sindar furent plus durables, notamment après les événements liés au Nauglamír.

Les Nains commercent volontiers avec les Hommes lorsqu’ils les jugent fiables et entretiennent généralement des rapports pacifiques avec les Hobbits. Leurs ennemis traditionnels comprennent surtout les Orcs, les Trolls, les Dragons et les créatures des profondeurs. Leur haine des Orcs est ancienne et liée aux guerres pour les montagnes, les mines et les forteresses.

Résistance à l’Ombre

Les Khazâd sont difficiles à soumettre par la domination mentale. Les Anneaux de Pouvoir donnés aux Nains ne firent pas d’eux des esclaves de Sauron comme les Neuf le firent des Hommes. Ils accrurent plutôt leur désir de richesse et leur avidité.

Cette résistance n’empêche pas la corruption par la cupidité, l’orgueil, la rancune ou l’obsession. La Race ne doit donc pas être considérée comme moralement protégée de l’Ombre.

Professions et place dans la création de personnage

La Race Khazâd — Naugrim est disponible durant les quatre Âges. Elle doit représenter les caractéristiques communes : petite taille, forte constitution, endurance, résistances, vision en faible lumière et sens de la pierre.

Les compétences de forge, de mine, de commerce, de guerre ou de magie doivent être précisées par la Culture. Après le choix de la Race, le joueur sélectionne une Maison ou une Culture correspondant à son origine, comme la Maison de Durin — Longues-Barbes ou les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár — Barbes-de-Feu et Torses-Larges.

Khazâd — Naugrim

The Khazâd, called Naugrim by the Elves, descend from the Seven Fathers fashioned from stone by the Vala Aulë. The Dwarves call Aulë Mahal, “the Maker”. He is the master of crafts, stone, metals and forges. The seven lineages descended from the Fathers settled in different regions, but always in or near mountains, which the Khazâd regard as sacred.

Aulë fashioned the Dwarves before the awakening of the Elves, but Eru required him to delay their awakening until after the appearance of the Firstborn. The Seven Fathers later awoke in different places. The most famous was Durin the Deathless, who awoke beneath Mount Gundabad before travelling south and founding Khazad-dûm.

The Seven Houses

The descendants of the Seven Fathers formed the great Dwarven Houses. Over the Ages, their members spread throughout Middle-earth, founding or occupying underground cities, mines and mountain settlements.

Each House possesses its own lineages, traditions, dialects, preferred crafts and histories. The Khazâd Race represents what is shared by all Dwarves; differences between the House of Durin, the Firebeards, the Broadbeams and the other lineages should be carried by Cultures.

Appearance

The Khazâd are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their bones are massive, their shoulders broad and their limbs exceptionally strong. They are heavy for their height. Men almost always wear beards, often long and maintained according to the customs of their House.

Dwarven women are fewer than men and rarely leave the dwellings of their people. They may also wear beards, which contributes to the difficulty outsiders have in immediately distinguishing the sexes. Hair, skin and eye colour vary according to lineage.

Longevity and maturity

The Khazâd live for several centuries. They reach maturity more slowly than Men and retain their strength and vigour for a long time. Their longevity allows them to devote decades to a work, know several human generations and preserve the memory of a debt, oath or insult for a very long time.

They nevertheless remain mortal. Their traditions teach that after death they are gathered to Mahal and that they will have a part to play in the restoration of Arda after its end.

Endurance and resistance

Dwarves are renowned for their endurance. They tolerate long marches, prolonged labour, heavy loads, cold, heat and deprivation well. Their constitution also makes them more resistant than ordinary Men to diseases and poisons.

This robustness is one of their principal racial traits. It should not, however, be confused with immunity: severe wounds, powerful diseases and sophisticated poisons can still kill them.

Vision and sense of stone

The Khazâd are adapted to underground life and see well in dim light. They know how to move and work in galleries where Men would require substantial illumination.

They also possess a remarkable sense for stone and underground works. An experienced Dwarf recognises the difference between natural rock and masonry, judges the stability of a gallery and readily notices unusual features in a wall, tunnel or stone construction. This ability should be represented as a common racial trait without replacing true skills in mining, architecture or stonecutting.

Temperament and memory

The Khazâd have a reputation for toughness, pragmatism, stubbornness and loyalty. They are generally cautious with strangers and place great value on clearly stated commitments.

They remember services rendered as well as offences for a long time. An agreement, debt, theft or oath may remain important for several generations. This memory feeds their reputation for bearing grudges, but also explains the solidity of their friendships and alliances once these have truly been established.

Lineage, family and authority

Family, clan and House occupy a central place in Dwarven society. A Khazâd generally knows their genealogy and the principal events concerning their ancestors. Crafts and certain secrets of workmanship are often passed down within families.

The kings of the great Houses represent the continuity of their lineages and dwellings. Among the Longbeards, the figure of Durin holds a special place. Marriage is monogamous and enduring; children are relatively rare and fiercely protected.

Craft and mining

The Khazâd are among the finest craftsmen of Middle-earth. They excel in smithcraft, metallurgy, armour-making, stonecutting, architecture, jewellery, engineering and mining. They seek gems and precious metals and transform them into tools, weapons, armour, jewellery and objects of exceptional quality.

Their craftsmanship favours strength and durability. A Dwarven work is generally intended to last for several generations. The working of matter is also closely connected to their reverence for Mahal.

Dwellings

The Khazâd favour rocky highlands, caverns and cities carved into mountains. Khazad-dûm was the most famous of their dwellings, but Nogrod, Belegost, Erebor, the Grey Mountains, the Iron Hills and many lesser-known settlements also belong to their history.

Their great mansions combine mines, workshops, halls, stores, fortifications, underground roads and living spaces. They are often designed so that they can be defended through narrow passages.

Language and writing

Khuzdul was taught to the Dwarves by Mahal. They guard it jealously and rarely reveal it to outsiders. True Khuzdul names are generally secret, and Dwarves often use names drawn from the languages of their neighbours when dealing with other peoples.

They readily use the Cirth to carve inscriptions into stone, metal, weapons, doors and tombs. Engraved writing suits their attachment to permanence and memory.

Religion

The Khazâd acknowledge Eru as the supreme Creator and deeply honour Mahal. Their religion is generally not organised around a visible clergy. It is expressed chiefly through reverence for ancestors, tombs, great dwellings, crafts and enduring works.

Forges, ancestral halls and royal tombs can possess a strong sacred dimension. The creation of an exceptional object may itself be regarded as a way of honouring Mahal.

Weapons, armour and war

Dwarves use many weapons, but axes, hammers, maces, swords, crossbows and polearms are especially common. They excel in making and wearing mail and heavy armour. Their strength and endurance allow them to remain effective under protection that would greatly slow other peoples.

They are particularly dangerous in defensive fighting, tunnels, gates, bridges and narrow passes. They know how to exploit confined approaches, close formations, shields, rockfalls and underground works.

Relations and enemies

Relations with the Elves have alternated between cooperation, trade and ancient conflict. The Noldor and the Khazâd have sometimes maintained especially fruitful relations because of their shared interest in craft and materials. Tensions with certain Sindar lasted longer, especially after the events surrounding the Nauglamír.

Dwarves willingly trade with Men they consider reliable and generally maintain peaceful relations with Hobbits. Their traditional enemies include chiefly Orcs, Trolls, Dragons and creatures of the deep. Their hatred of Orcs is ancient and rooted in wars over mountains, mines and fortresses.

Resistance to the Shadow

The Khazâd are difficult to subdue through mental domination. The Rings of Power given to the Dwarves did not make them slaves of Sauron as the Nine did the Men who bore them. Instead, they increased their desire for wealth and their greed.

This resistance does not prevent corruption through avarice, pride, resentment or obsession. The Race should therefore not be regarded as morally protected from the Shadow.

Professions and place in character creation

The Khazâd — Naugrim Race is available throughout all four Ages. It should represent the shared traits of the Dwarves: short stature, strong constitution, endurance, resistances, vision in dim light and sense of stone.

Skills in smithing, mining, trade, warfare or magic should be specified by Culture. After choosing the Race, the player selects a House or Culture corresponding to the character’s origin, such as the House of Durin — Longbeards or the Houses of Dwálin and Thrár — Firebeards and Broadbeams.

system.description:
Humains — Hildor

Les Humains, appelés Hildor par les Elfes, sont les Seconds-Nés des Enfants d’Ilúvatar. Ils s’éveillèrent dans l’Est de la Terre du Milieu, dans une région appelée Hildórien, au cours du Premier Âge. Les Elfes les nommèrent Hildor, « les Suivants », parce qu’ils apparurent après les Premiers-Nés. Les termes quenya Atani et sindarin Edain, « Second Peuple », furent également employés pour les désigner.

Les Hommes diffèrent des Elfes avant tout par le Don des Hommes : ils sont mortels. Leur vie est brève à l’échelle des Elfes et des Nains, mais ils se renouvellent rapidement, fondent de nouvelles communautés et s’adaptent à des environnements très différents. Ils sont nombreux, variés et plus vulnérables que les Elfes aux maladies et aux températures extrêmes, mais ils se lassent rarement de la vie.

Origines et diversité

Les premiers siècles de l’histoire humaine sont mal connus dans l’Ouest. Les Hommes se dispersèrent très tôt et leurs peuples développèrent des langues, des coutumes et des modes de vie distincts. Lorsque certains atteignirent le Beleriand, plusieurs lignées existaient déjà.

Cette diversité est un caractère essentiel des Hildor. La Race représente donc la nature humaine commune, tandis que les Cultures déterminent l’éducation, la langue, les compétences, les croyances et les usages d’un personnage. Un Rohirrim, un Beffraen, un Dorwinrim, un Haruze, un Variag ou un Homme des Bois sont tous des Humains, même si leurs sociétés et leurs aptitudes culturelles diffèrent fortement.

Le Don des Hommes

Les Hommes sont mortels et leur destin après la mort est différent de celui des Elfes. Dans la tradition des Sages, cette mortalité est un don d’Ilúvatar et non une imperfection. Les esprits des Hommes quittent les limites du monde selon une destinée que les Valar eux-mêmes ne connaissent pas pleinement.

La conscience de cette mortalité influence fortement les sociétés humaines. Elle peut favoriser l’ambition, le désir de descendance, la volonté de laisser une œuvre durable ou la recherche de gloire. Elle peut aussi engendrer la peur de la mort et le désir de prolonger artificiellement la vie. Sauron exploita souvent cette faiblesse, notamment chez les Númenóréens.

Grands groupes humains

Les traditions occidentales distinguent les Hauts Hommes, les Hommes communs et parfois les Hommes du Nord. Les Hauts Hommes descendent des Edain alliés aux Elfes contre Morgoth et sont à l’origine des Númenóréens puis des Dúnedain. Dans merp-ui, les Dúnedain sont traités comme une Race distincte afin de représenter leur longévité, leur stature et leur héritage particuliers.

Les Hommes communs représentent la majorité des peuples humains. Leur apparence et leurs cultures sont extrêmement diverses. Les Hommes du Nord sont proches de certaines lignées des Edain, mais n’ont pas bénéficié du même contact prolongé avec les Eldar ni des dons accordés aux habitants de Númenor.

Apparence

Les Humains présentent la plus grande diversité physique parmi les principales Races jouables. Leur taille, leur corpulence, la couleur de leur peau, de leurs cheveux et de leurs yeux varient selon les peuples et les régions. Les Hommes communs sont en moyenne plus petits et plus trapus que les Dúnedain, mais aucune apparence unique ne peut être considérée comme typiquement humaine.

Les cheveux peuvent être noirs, bruns, châtains, roux ou blonds. Les yeux peuvent être noirs, bruns, gris, bleus, verts ou noisette. La pilosité faciale est courante chez de nombreuses populations masculines. Les différences physiques doivent être déterminées par la Culture et l’origine régionale plutôt que par un modèle racial unique.

Longévité, maturité et santé

La plupart des Hommes vivent entre cinquante et quatre-vingts ans, bien que l’espérance de vie varie fortement selon les conditions de vie et les lignées. Certains individus dépassent quatre-vingt-dix ans. Les Hommes atteignent leur maturité beaucoup plus rapidement que les Elfes et les Nains, ce qui leur permet de renouveler rapidement leurs générations.

Ils sont sensibles aux maladies, aux infections, aux poisons et aux températures extrêmes. Cette vulnérabilité les a conduits à développer de nombreuses traditions de médecine, d’herboristerie et de soins. Les résistances particulières au froid, à la chaleur, aux maladies ou aux privations doivent provenir d’une Culture, d’un Talent ou de l’équipement plutôt que de la Race elle-même.

Endurance, sommeil et sens

L’endurance humaine est moyenne mais très variable. Des soldats, cavaliers, marins, chasseurs ou voyageurs entraînés peuvent soutenir des efforts importants pendant de longues périodes. Leur capacité à supporter la fatigue dépend largement de l’entraînement et de la volonté.

Les Humains ont besoin d’un sommeil régulier et ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Leur vision, leur ouïe et leurs autres sens se situent dans la moyenne. Une aptitude supérieure à la perception, au pistage ou à la survie doit donc être apportée par la Culture ou l’apprentissage.

Adaptabilité

La principale caractéristique des Humains est leur capacité à s’adapter rapidement. Ils vivent dans les plaines, les montagnes, les forêts, les déserts, les régions froides, les marais, les côtes et les grandes cités. En quelques générations, une communauté peut modifier son habitat, son alimentation, ses techniques de guerre, ses institutions et sa langue pour répondre à un nouvel environnement.

Cette faculté explique la grande variété des sociétés humaines. Les Hildor peuvent former des villages agricoles, des tribus nomades, des cités marchandes, des royaumes féodaux, des sociétés pastorales ou des empires centralisés.

Famille et société

Les Humains ont généralement davantage d’enfants que les Elfes ou les Nains. Les formes de famille, les règles de mariage, les successions et la place des clans varient considérablement d’une Culture à l’autre. La Race humaine n’impose donc pas de structure familiale particulière.

Il en va de même pour les formes de gouvernement. Les Hommes peuvent vivre sous l’autorité d’un chef de clan, d’un conseil, d’un roi, d’un prince, d’une cité autonome ou d’une administration complexe. Les institutions humaines évoluent rapidement à l’échelle de l’histoire de la Terre du Milieu.

Artisanat, techniques et guerre

Les Hommes peuvent atteindre un haut niveau d’artisanat, d’ingénierie et d’organisation. Ils pratiquent l’agriculture, la métallurgie, la construction, la navigation, l’élevage, le commerce et la fortification. Ils ne possèdent pas l’affinité particulière des Khazâd avec la pierre et le métal ni l’ancien savoir des Eldar, mais ils diffusent rapidement les techniques nouvelles.

Ils ont développé presque toutes les formes de guerre connues : infanterie, cavalerie, archers, lanciers, marins, éclaireurs et troupes lourdes. Les armes et armures favorites dépendent entièrement de la Culture et des ressources disponibles.

Il n’existe pas de langue humaine unique. Le westron devient la principale langue commune du nord-ouest de la Terre du Milieu aux Âges tardifs, mais l’adûnaïque, le rohirrique, le dunael, le haradaïque, le varadja, le logathig, le nahaiduk et de nombreux autres parlers restent liés à des peuples particuliers.

Les croyances humaines sont tout aussi diverses. Certains peuples reconnaissent clairement Eru et les Valar ; d’autres ont conservé des traditions anciennes ou développé des religions locales. Certaines sociétés ont également subi l’influence de Morgoth ou de Sauron. Les Humains peuvent pratiquer toutes les grandes formes de magie prévues par RMU lorsque leur Culture et leur formation le permettent.

Les rapports entre les Hommes et les Elfes vont de l’alliance étroite à la méfiance. Les relations avec les Khazâd sont souvent fondées sur le commerce, les métaux, les outils et les produits agricoles. Les Hobbits vivent généralement en paix avec les communautés humaines voisines.

Les Hommes occupent aussi une place centrale dans les guerres de l’Ombre. Certains furent parmi les plus grands adversaires de Morgoth et de Sauron, tandis que d’autres devinrent leurs serviteurs. Les Nazgûl eux-mêmes étaient autrefois des Hommes.

Humans — Hildor

Humans, called Hildor by the Elves, are the Secondborn of the Children of Ilúvatar. They awoke in the East of Middle-earth, in a land called Hildórien, during the First Age. The Elves named them Hildor, “the Followers”, because they appeared after the Firstborn. The Quenya term Atani and the Sindarin Edain, “Second People”, were also used for them.

Humans differ from Elves above all through the Gift of Men: they are mortal. Their lives are brief by the measure of Elves and Dwarves, yet their generations renew quickly, they establish new communities, and they adapt to widely different environments. They are numerous and diverse, more vulnerable than Elves to disease and extremes of climate, but they rarely grow weary of life.

Origins and diversity

The first centuries of human history are poorly known in the West. Men dispersed early, and their peoples developed distinct languages, customs, and ways of life. By the time some reached Beleriand, several lineages already existed.

This diversity is essential to the Hildor. The Race therefore represents shared human nature, while Cultures determine a character’s upbringing, language, skills, beliefs, and customs. A Rohir, Beffraen, Dorwinrim, Haruze, Variag, or Woodman are all Humans even though their societies and cultural abilities differ greatly.

The Gift of Men

Men are mortal, and their fate after death differs from that of the Elves. In the tradition of the Wise, mortality is a gift of Ilúvatar rather than an imperfection. The spirits of Men leave the bounds of the world according to a destiny that even the Valar do not fully know.

Awareness of mortality strongly shapes human societies. It may foster ambition, the desire for descendants, the wish to leave an enduring work, or the pursuit of glory. It can also create fear of death and the desire to prolong life unnaturally. Sauron often exploited this weakness, most notably among the Númenóreans.

Major human groups

Western traditions distinguish High Men, Common Men, and sometimes Northmen. High Men descend from the Edain who allied with the Elves against Morgoth and became the ancestors of the Númenóreans and later the Dúnedain. In MERP-UI, the Dúnedain are treated as a separate Race to represent their particular longevity, stature, and heritage.

Common Men make up most human peoples. Their appearances and cultures are extraordinarily varied. Northmen are close to some lineages of the Edain, but they did not benefit from the same prolonged contact with the Eldar or from the gifts granted to the people of Númenor.

Appearance

Humans show the greatest physical diversity among the principal playable Races. Height, build, skin tone, hair, and eye colour vary by people and region. Common Men are on average shorter and stockier than the Dúnedain, but no single appearance can be considered typically human.

Hair may be black, brown, chestnut, red, or blond. Eyes may be black, brown, grey, blue, green, or hazel. Facial hair is common among many male populations. Physical differences should be determined by Culture and regional origin rather than by a single racial model.

Longevity, maturity, and health

Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

They are susceptible to disease, infection, poison, and extremes of temperature. This vulnerability has led to many traditions of medicine, herbalism, and healing. Particular resistance to cold, heat, disease, or deprivation should come from Culture, a Talent, or equipment rather than from the Race itself.

Endurance, sleep, and senses

Human endurance is average but highly variable. Trained soldiers, riders, sailors, hunters, and travellers can sustain considerable effort for long periods. Their ability to withstand fatigue depends largely on training and willpower.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

Adaptability

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

This ability explains the great variety of human societies. The Hildor may form farming villages, nomadic tribes, trading cities, feudal kingdoms, pastoral societies, or centralized empires.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Crafts, technology, and war

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

Languages, religion, and magic

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

In MERP-UI, the Dúnedain are treated as a separate Race to represent their particular longevity, stature, and heritage.

Common Men make up most human peoples. Their appearances and cultures are extraordinarily varied. Northmen are close to some lineages of the Edain, but they did not benefit from the same prolonged contact with the Eldar or from the gifts granted to the people of Númenor.

Appearance

Humans show the greatest physical diversity among the principal playable Races. Height, build, skin tone, hair, and eye colour vary by people and region. Common Men are on average shorter and stockier than the Dúnedain, but no single appearance can be considered typically human.

Hair may be black, brown, chestnut, red, or blond. Eyes may be black, brown, grey, blue, green, or hazel. Facial hair is common among many male populations. Physical differences should be determined by Culture and regional origin rather than by a single racial model.

Longevity, maturity, and health

Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

They are susceptible to disease, infection, poison, and extremes of temperature. This vulnerability has led to many traditions of medicine, herbalism, and healing. Particular resistance to cold, heat, disease, or deprivation should come from Culture, a Talent, or equipment rather than from the Race itself.

Endurance, sleep, and senses

Human endurance is average but highly variable. Trained soldiers, riders, sailors, hunters, and travellers can sustain considerable effort for long periods. Their ability to withstand fatigue depends largely on training and willpower.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

Adaptability

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

This ability explains the great variety of human societies. The Hildor may form farming villages, nomadic tribes, trading cities, feudal kingdoms, pastoral societies, or centralized empires.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Crafts, technology, and war

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.
